clue.text: It's agreed to include name of knight in dictionary

indicators.note: to include tells us the dictionary wraps round the knight's name

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
Sir Kay is a knight of King Arthur's Round Table

explanation.surface: An official announcement that a knight's name has been accepted into the dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Kay is Arthur's foster-brother in the legends, which makes him a well-known crossword knight.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something approved or given the nod has been agreed.

clue.text: Description of blood type initially indicates relationship by blood

indicators.note: initially says the word for type comes at the front, ahead of the colour

parts.note: a type is a kind or sort
blood is described as red

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding note about how a blood group points to family ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blood type' looks like one phrase, but it splits: 'Description of blood' is the colour and 'type' is a separate synonym. 'Indicates' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun this word means kinship, the tie between relatives who share descent.

clue.text: Many a hooligan's one

definitions.note: a lout or boor is often called by this name, from the brutish creatures in Swift's Gulliver's Travels

indicators.note: the 's is read as 'has', so the words before it have the answer held within them

explanation.surface: A sweeping remark that plenty of hooligans are a certain sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Many a hooligan's one' as 'Many a hooligan has one': the word sits across 'manY A HOOligan', and the whole clue also defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a rude, loutish brute, from Swift's Gulliver's Travels, which describes most hooligans.

clue.text: 27 2 15 book featuring Deidre (in Chelmsford postcode area) on the loose

indicators.note: on the loose means running wild, so all these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A novel about a woman called Deidre who is running wild around Chelmsford, an Essex town.
explanation.walkthrough: '27 2 15' points to the author Philip K. Dick through those answers. The fodder is all thirty letters of 'Deidre in Chelmsford postcode area'; the brackets are only surface. 'Featuring' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip K. Dick's 1968 science-fiction novel, filmed as Blade Runner, is the book meant.

clue.text: I hate this time, being overwhelmed by a lot of those ideas

indicators.note: being overwhelmed by puts the cry of disgust and the time inside the shortened word
a lot of means most of the word, leaving off its final letter

parts.note: ugh is the cry of someone who hates something

explanation.surface: Someone groans that they hate this period and feel swamped by all those ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of those' gives THOS, and UGH plus T go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple plural synonym: ideas are notions that come to mind.

clue.text: Crushed apricot's not right with a pudding

indicators.note: crushed fruit is mashed up, so the letters left are rearranged
not here means the letter for right is left out of the fruit

parts.note: the fruit's name, with 's read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A recipe note: crushed apricot that has gone wrong, served with a pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apricot's not right' means apricot is without R: APICOT, which 'Crushed' rearranges into TAPIOC before A is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapioca, made from cassava starch, is a classic British milk pudding.

clue.text: See 4
Slides showing openings outside orbiter

indicators.note: outside says the clearings go round the space station

parts.note: glades are clearings or openings in a forest
the ISS, the International Space Station, orbits the Earth

explanation.surface: Photographic slides that show the openings around a spacecraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Openings' suggests gaps or starts, but here it means forest clearings.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet, skiing and climbing, these are gliding movements or controlled slides.

clue.text: Ill-fated vessel at sea? I can't take it in

indicators.note: take means take in, so the rearranged letters hold the little word
at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone thinks about a doomed ship and admits they cannot take in the thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' rearranges I CANT into TANIC, and 'take' puts IT inside it; 'in' finishes the phrase 'take in'.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous liner sank on its maiden voyage in 1912, the best-known doomed ship of all.

clue.text: Half this measure would be appropriate

definitions.text: Half this measure would be appropriate

parts.words: Half this measure would be appropriate
parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang, putting the word half in front of this unit of length gives rhyming slang for to steal or appropriate

explanation.surface: Someone suggests that only half of a certain measure would be suitable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as 'suitable' but means 'steal'. 'Half-inch' is Cockney rhyming slang for pinch, i.e. steal, so half of this measure is the slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: The measure is the imperial length of 2.54 centimetres, and 'half' of it gives the slang verb for stealing.

clue.text: Go up and see

definitions.meaning: to rise in value, as property or shares do over time
to understand or recognise fully, as in grasping a point

explanation.surface: A short instruction to climb and take a look.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both rising in value and recognising or understanding something.

clue.text: Old composer? Not English old composer

indicators.note: not English means the abbreviation for English is dropped from the old composer

parts.note: Thomas Arne was an 18th-century English composer, of Rule, Britannia!
taken as written

explanation.surface: A quiz-style question: is the old composer meant? No, not the English old composer.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'old composer' tempts a single reading, but the first 'Old' is the letters themselves and the second phrase is ARNE, losing E to give ARN.
explanation.definitionFit: Malcolm Arnold was a 20th-century English composer known for film scores and symphonies.

clue.text: Respectful order is given to soldier?

parts.note: the OBE is the Order of the British Empire
taken as written
a soldier ant is one of the colony's fighting caste

explanation.surface: A question of whether a soldier must show respect when given an order.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'soldier' is an insect, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: being deferential means showing obedience and respect.

clue.text: Mum perhaps gets too darned cross

indicators.note: cross suggests things crossed over and mixed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mother becomes extremely annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother, but Mum is a British brand of underarm product, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mum is a long-standing brand name, an example of this kind of toiletry.

clue.text: As soon as one returns afresh

parts.note: once can mean as soon as, as in once you arrive
a means one
returns on an investment are gains

explanation.surface: A remark about something starting anew the moment someone comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' looks like a reversal signal, but it is a noun meaning profits.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean repeating something over again, from the start.

clue.text: A plonker taken in by David Icke

indicators.note: taken in by says the word is held within the name that follows

explanation.surface: A fool is duped by David Icke, the British conspiracy theorist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plonker' is British slang for an idiot, and so is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are coarse British slang terms for a stupid or contemptible person.

clue.text: Lack of completion in building coalition

indicators.note: lack of completion means the word is not finished, so its last letter goes

parts.note: a block is a large building, such as an office block

explanation.surface: A building that isn't finished, set in the context of a coalition.
explanation.walkthrough: BLOCK loses its last letter because it is not completed; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of nations or parties allied for a common aim is called a bloc.

clue.text: Without question, I rule out alcoholic drink

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the rearranged letters surround the abbreviation
out means put out of order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone firmly swears off alcohol, ruling out drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means 'outside', not 'lacking': I RULE is rearranged ('out') into LIEUR, which goes around QU.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet, flavoured spirit such as Cointreau is a classic example of this drink.

clue.text: Special teacher, having pierced face, gets the sack

indicators.note: having pierced says these pieces go through and into the clock face

parts.note: a dial is a clock face
Miss is how pupils address a female teacher

explanation.surface: A teacher with a facial piercing gets fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face' is the dial of a clock, not a person's face.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the sack is British slang for being fired from a job.

clue.text: Big cat with upset stomach after gentleman gives steak

indicators.note: after puts the cat's letters behind the title

parts.note: Sir is the title for a knighted gentleman

indicators.note: upset stomach means the middle of the cat's name is turned over

parts.note: a lion is a big cat

explanation.surface: A lion with a bad stomach follows a gentleman who is handing out steak.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the 'stomach' of LION, its middle IO, is turned over, giving LOIN.
explanation.definitionFit: This prime cut from the upper loin of beef is a well-known steak.

clue.text: Seductress learning to sleep in regularly

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge or learning

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the words

explanation.surface: A temptress who is learning to lie in on a regular basis.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of 'sleep in' give LEI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei is a Rhine siren whose singing lured boatmen to their deaths.

clue.text: Short podgy nerd, sad and blue

indicators.note: short means the word is cut, losing its last letter

parts.note: squat means short and podgy

indicators.note: sad means pathetic or messed up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cruel description of a little, overweight geek who is sad and depressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' looks like a sad mood to match the surface, but in British slang to blue money is to blow it.
explanation.definitionFit: To blue money is old British slang for spending it recklessly, i.e. wasting it.

clue.text: Scoundrel cracks bishop's office safe

indicators.note: cracks means breaks into, so the rogue goes inside

parts.note: a see is a bishop's seat or diocese
a cur is a contemptible man

explanation.surface: A villain breaks into the bishop's office safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe' looks like the strongbox being cracked, but it is the adjective meaning protected.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: protected from danger or harm.

clue.text: Animal pet, one with nothing to eat

indicators.note: to eat means swallow, so the pet and one take in the zero

parts.note: a cat is a household pet
O looks like zero, nothing
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A pet animal is left with nothing to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The coati is a South American raccoon relative with a long snout.
explanation.definitionFit: The coati is a mammal of the raccoon family, so an example of an animal.

clue.text: Aeneas when adrift receives warning sign about tentacled creature

indicators.note: receives means the rearranged name takes the reversed word inside it
when adrift means drifting loose, so the hero's letters are rearranged
about means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: an omen is a sign of things to come, often a warning

explanation.surface: The Trojan hero Aeneas, lost at sea, meets a monster after a bad omen.
explanation.walkthrough: AENEAS is rearranged ('when adrift') into SEAA...NE, and 'about' turns OMEN into NEMO, which sits inside.
explanation.definitionFit: This sea creature is a polyp with a ring of stinging tentacles.

clue.text: Competent firm? No way

indicators.note: no means the abbreviation for way is taken away

parts.note: stable means firm and steady
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a firm is competent, and the answer is no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company, but it is the adjective meaning steady.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple synonym: capable or skilled enough to do something.

clue.text: Lead singer of group from Angola devouring books

indicators.note: devouring means the word swallows the books, which go inside it

parts.note: taken as written
NT is the New Testament, a collection of books of the Bible
AN is taken as a code for Angola

explanation.surface: A band's lead singer who comes from Angola and reads voraciously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' looks like a link word, but its letters are the container; NT for books is a crossword standard.
explanation.definitionFit: The lead singer is the member who fronts a band, the face of the group.

clue.text: Prince given a boost on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio means heard rather than seen, so we go by sound

parts.note: a fillip is a stimulus or boost

explanation.surface: A royal gets some encouragement during a broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Philip was the late Duke of Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, was the Queen's husband.
